sectionTitle: Physics — Waves in air, fluids and solids: Transverse and longitudinal waves

specStatements.text: Waves may be either transverse or longitudinal.
The ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave.
Longitudinal waves show areas of compression and rarefaction. Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal.
Students should be able to describe the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves.
Students should be able to describe evidence that, for both ripples on a water surface and sound waves in air, it is the wave and not the water or air itself that travels.

concepts.definition: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. Ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave.
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal waves show areas of compression and rarefaction, and sound travelling through air is longitudinal.

The repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down movement of a particle of the medium about a fixed position as a wave passes. The direction of this oscillation compared with the direction the wave travels is what separates the two types of wave.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are pushed closer together than normal, so the medium there is at a higher pressure.

A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are spread further apart than normal, so the medium there is at a lower pressure. The particles are still present; a rarefaction is not an empty space.
A wave on a water surface. Each part of the surface moves up and down while the ripple travels outwards, which is what makes it a transverse wave.
A longitudinal wave in which the air is repeatedly pushed together and pulled apart, producing compressions and rarefactions that travel away from the source.
A wave moves energy from place to place while the water or air it passes through only oscillates about a fixed position and is not carried along with the wave.

misconceptions.question: As ripples cross a pond, what happens to the water itself?
misconceptions.correct: Each part of the surface moves up and down about a fixed position while the ripple travels outwards.
misconceptions.misconception: The water is carried along with the ripple, so water from the middle of the pond ends up at the bank.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ripples look like humps of water sliding across the surface, and in everyday speech a 'wave' at the seaside really is water rushing up a beach.
misconceptions.correction: A floating ball bobs up and down in the same place as ripple after ripple passes under it. It is not carried to the far bank, so only the wave crosses the pond.

misconceptions.question: Does air travel from a loudspeaker to your ear when you hear a sound?
misconceptions.correct: No. The air oscillates back and forth about a fixed position; the wave travels, the air does not.
misconceptions.misconception: The loudspeaker pushes a stream of air across the room and that moving air reaches your ear as the sound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know sound needs air, and a moving speaker cone does push on the air, so they picture a puff of air travelling all the way to the listener.
misconceptions.correction: No draught is felt from a loudspeaker playing music, and a candle flame in front of it is not blown out. The air near the cone simply oscillates and passes the disturbance on.

misconceptions.question: Is a sound wave in air transverse or longitudinal?
misconceptions.correct: Longitudinal — the air oscillates along the direction in which the sound travels.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound is transverse, because it is drawn and displayed as a wavy line with crests and troughs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oscilloscope traces and the waveforms shown by recording software are drawn as curves, and students read the shape of the graph as the shape of the wave.
misconceptions.correction: The curve is a graph of pressure or displacement against time, not a picture of the air. The air itself is pushed together and pulled apart along the direction of travel.

misconceptions.question: What is a rarefaction in a sound wave?
misconceptions.correct: A region where the air particles are spread further apart than normal, at a lower pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: A rarefaction is an empty gap in the air, a small vacuum with no particles in it at all; or it is simply the same thing as a compression.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Particle diagrams show rarefactions as noticeably emptier bands, and the two long words are easily swapped when they are learned as a pair.
misconceptions.correction: The particles are only spread out, never removed. A rarefaction is a region of lower pressure that still contains air; a compression is the opposite, where the air is squashed together.

misconceptions.question: In which direction do the particles oscillate in each type of wave?
misconceptions.correct: Parallel to the direction of energy transfer in a longitudinal wave, perpendicular to it in a transverse wave.
misconceptions.misconception: The two are the other way round: longitudinal means the oscillations are across the direction of travel and transverse means along it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are learned as a pair without being tied to their meanings, so students remember that there is a contrast but not which label goes with which motion.
misconceptions.correction: Link the word to its meaning: 'longitudinal' shares its root with 'along', so the oscillation is along the direction of travel; 'transverse' shares its root with 'across'.

misconceptions.question: What decides whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of the oscillations compared with the direction in which the wave travels.
misconceptions.misconception: It depends on how the wave is drawn: a curvy line means transverse and a row of lines means longitudinal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Each type is met through one standard diagram, so the diagram style becomes the definition rather than an illustration of it.
misconceptions.correction: The same wave can be represented in several ways. Ask what the particles of the medium are doing, not what the picture looks like.

misconceptions.question: Can a longitudinal wave travel through air?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal.
misconceptions.misconception: Longitudinal waves need a solid such as a slinky, so a wave travelling through air must be transverse.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Longitudinal waves are usually demonstrated on a slinky, so students attach the wave type to the springy solid used in the demonstration.
misconceptions.correction: Any material that can be compressed can carry a longitudinal wave. Air is squeezed and stretched by a loudspeaker exactly as the slinky is by a hand.

misconceptions.question: Are all waves transverse?
misconceptions.correct: No. Waves may be either transverse or longitudinal.
misconceptions.misconception: Every wave is transverse, because a wave is that wavy shape with crests and troughs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'wave' is bound to a picture of a wavy curve from primary school onwards, and that picture is a transverse one.
misconceptions.correction: The wavy curve is only one type. Sound in air is longitudinal, with compressions and rarefactions instead of crests and troughs.

misconceptions.question: What does a wave transfer from one place to another?
misconceptions.correct: Energy. The medium is left where it was once the wave has passed.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave has to carry the material along with it, because something must physically move for anything to arrive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday transport moves the stuff as well as the effect, so students assume that delivering energy means delivering matter.
misconceptions.correction: Each particle passes the disturbance on to its neighbour and returns to its own position, so energy arrives while the medium stays where it was.

misconceptions.question: Does a floating object drift forwards as ripples pass beneath it?
misconceptions.correct: No. It bobs up and down about the same position while the ripples move on.
misconceptions.misconception: Each passing ripple nudges the float a little further forwards, so it slowly drifts to the far side.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Floats on a real pond do drift because of wind and currents, and students credit the ripples with the movement they can see.
misconceptions.correction: In still water the float returns to the same place after every ripple. Any drift is caused by wind or a current, not by the wave itself.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the types of wave is correct?

options.text: A wave may be either transverse or longitudinal.
options.rationale: The specification states that waves may be either transverse or longitudinal, so both types exist.

options.text: Every wave is transverse, as the diagrams show.
options.rationale: Chosen by students whose mental image of a wave is the wavy curve, which makes every wave look transverse.

options.text: The type depends on how the wave gets drawn.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who learned each type from one standard diagram and treat the drawing style as the definition.

options.text: Water waves are the only transverse waves.
options.rationale: Ripples are the example given for a transverse wave, so students take the single example to be the only case.

mcqs.stem: Ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave. Why?

options.text: The water surface oscillates back and forth along the direction the ripple travels.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have swapped the two definitions and think transverse means oscillating along the direction of travel.

options.text: The water surface oscillates up and down, across the direction the ripple moves.
options.rationale: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, which is what the surface does.

options.text: The water is carried forwards across the pond as every ripple passes it.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe the water travels with the ripple, and who use that motion to classify the wave.

options.text: The ripple is always drawn as a curved line in the textbook diagrams.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who classify a wave from the shape of its picture rather than from the motion of the medium.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave travels through air. What is a rarefaction in this wave?

options.text: A region where the air particles are pushed together.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have swapped the two terms; this describes a compression, not a rarefaction.

options.text: A region where the air particles move across the wave.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture sound as transverse and so expect sideways motion of the air.

options.text: A region where the air particles are further apart.
options.rationale: A rarefaction is where the particles of the medium are spread out, giving a lower pressure than normal.

options.text: A region of empty space with no air particles.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read the gaps in a particle diagram as a small vacuum rather than as spread-out air.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a sound wave travelling through air is correct?

options.text: It is transverse, because it is displayed as a wavy trace.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read an oscilloscope trace as a picture of the air rather than as a graph against time.

options.text: It is longitudinal, so it must have a solid to travel through.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who tie longitudinal waves to the slinky used to demonstrate them and so rule out air.

options.text: It is transverse, with crests and troughs of moving air.
options.rationale: Chosen by students for whom every wave has crests and troughs, so sound must have them too.

options.text: It is longitudinal, with compressions and rarefactions.
options.rationale: Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal, and longitudinal waves show areas of compression and rarefaction.

mcqs.stem: What is the difference between a longitudinal wave and a transverse wave?

options.text: A longitudinal wave carries the material of the medium along with it, while a transverse wave carries only the energy.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a compression must shift the medium forwards while a transverse wave does not.

options.text: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of travel, and in a transverse wave they are perpendicular to it.
options.rationale: This is the defining difference: the two types are separated by the direction of the oscillations relative to the direction of travel.

options.text: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel, and in a transverse wave they are parallel.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember that there is a contrast between the two words but have attached each label to the wrong motion.

options.text: A longitudinal wave is drawn as a row of straight lines, while a transverse wave is always drawn as a wavy curve.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who define the two types by their standard diagrams rather than by the motion of the particles.

mcqs.stem: One end of a long slinky is pushed and pulled repeatedly along its length. Which description of the wave produced is correct?

options.text: Longitudinal, because the coils vibrate along the direction the wave travels.
options.rationale: Pushing and pulling along the slinky makes the coils oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer, giving compressions and rarefactions.

options.text: Transverse, because the coils vibrate across the direction that the wave travels.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have swapped the two definitions, so they label an along-the-slinky oscillation as transverse.

options.text: Longitudinal, because the coils are carried along to the far end of it.
options.rationale: The wave type is right but the reason is wrong: each coil oscillates about its own position and no coil travels the length of the slinky.

options.text: Transverse, because a moving bunch of coils is seen along the slinky.
options.rationale: Chosen by students for whom any visible travelling shape means a transverse wave.

mcqs.stem: A ball floats on a still pond while ripples pass beneath it. Which observation is evidence that the water itself does not travel?

options.text: The ball is carried away to the far bank by ripples.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe the water moves along with the ripple, taking floating objects with it.

options.text: The ball edges a little further forwards as each ripple passes.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who credit the ripples with the slow drift that wind or a current would cause.

options.text: The far side of the pond becomes deeper as the ripples arrive.
options.rationale: What a student who thinks the water is carried along would predict: water piling up where the ripples end up.

options.text: The ball bobs up and down but stays in the same place.
options.rationale: The float returns to its position after every ripple, showing that the wave passes through the water while the water stays put.

mcqs.stem: A loudspeaker plays loud music. Which observation is evidence that the air itself does not travel across the room to the listener?

options.text: A steady breeze can be felt coming from the loudspeaker cone.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture a stream of air being pushed across the room; a real loudspeaker produces no such breeze.

options.text: A candle flame placed in front of the loudspeaker is blown out.
options.rationale: The prediction made by students who think moving air carries the sound; the flame in fact stays lit.

options.text: No draught is felt by the listener as the music plays.
options.rationale: If air travelled across the room there would be a draught. The air only oscillates and passes the disturbance on.

options.text: The music is heard a moment after the cone starts moving.
options.rationale: A real observation, but it is evidence that the wave takes time to travel, not evidence about whether the air moves with it.
